newsitem.title: INDIA: FUND VIEW-India share cool down offers bargains(RPT).
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-India share cool down offers bargains(RPT).

text.p: India's boiling stock market is showing signs of cooling after an eight-month-long rally but fund managers said it was a good opportunity to accumulate shares.
"Far from an over-bought zone the market is hardly in a bought zone," said Bharat Shah, chief investment officer at Birla Capital International AMC Ltd.
"There's lot of money in the banks waiting to enter the markets which indicates that the market is substantially underbought as yet," he said.
The benchmark 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index last week ended 76.66 points, or 1.75 percent, lower at 4,320.97 -- after surging to 34-month highs more than two weeks ago.
Analysts expect the market to be range-bound at 4,200-4,400 points until December, because of new equity issues in the pipeline and discouraging by lower first half results.

Two large state-run firms, Gas Authority of India and Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd, have plans to raise about $1.5 billion through an international issue of global depositary receipts in the last quarter of 1997.

"Worries on interim results accompanied by earnings downgrades and increased stock supply .. are expected to lead to a downward correction (in the short-term)," said Jyotivardhan Jaipuria, strategist at Merrill Lynch's Indian affiliate.
But the market was currently trading at price earnings multiple of 16.2 times the historic earnings against a five-year average of 27.9, he said.
S.K. Mitra, a director at Birla Capital, believes this is the right time for investors to buy.
"Time is running out for retail investors," he said. "They should come in now rather than jump in when the market is really hot."
Birla Capital is a Mauritius-registered joint venture, between India's Aditya Birla Group and Capital Group of the U.S., which manages about 5.9 billion rupees ($165 million).

A $10 million open-ended offshore India Advantage Fund it launched a year ago has swelled 56 percent to $15.6 million, Shah said, adding that it outperformed the BSE index's 29 percent rise in the same period.
His success was based on buying into a company which offered good valuations, irrespective of the sector it was in.
Shah said a poorly faring industry sometimes offered the best bargains like chemical firm Clariant India Ltd, a subsidiary of Clariant AG.
"Our methodology is: You can lose out on an excellent stock in a badly faring industry, and you can end up buying a very lousy firm in an exciting industry," he said.
DSP Merrill Lynch's Jaipuria expects the market rally to spill over to the broader section and advised clients to look at sectors that face bad news in the near-term.
He said in a note that he has upgraded engineering and finance sectors to overweight from neutral, and sees opportunities in cement shares.
"We are adding India Cements to our top picks, given our increased weighting of the cement sector, and Tata Power given its sharp underperformance," he said.
Fund managers must look to 1998 when an economic revival is forecast to boost the BSE index to 5,000-5,200 points, he added.
